hypotheses.title: SCReAM uses less of the link than GCC when the network drops capacity
hypotheses.claim: When the network's bandwidth drops sharply, SCReAM sends less than GCC does — at least on the runs we tested.

established: Whether SCReAM or GCC sends more during the low-capacity phase depends on how fast the bandwidth changes.
What the sender pushes onto the wire and what the viewer actually receives are two different questions: this hypothesis is about the sender.
limits: This is not a general claim that one algorithm is better than the other.

hypotheses.title: On a wobbly network, GCC delivers more frames than SCReAM regardless of deadline or retransmit settings
hypotheses.claim: When the link's bandwidth keeps changing, the viewer gets more frames with GCC than with SCReAM, and turning retransmits on or off or tightening the late-frame deadline does not change which one wins.

established: GCC delivers more median frames than SCReAM in every combination of deadline and retransmit we tested on this wobbly network.
Adding retransmits or tightening the late-frame deadline does not change which algorithm wins.
limits: This is a result for one wobbly network, not a general claim about retransmits or deadlines on every network.

hypotheses.title: The test video is too lightweight to compare SCReAM and GCC on 5G recordings
hypotheses.claim: The current test video (ball-720p30) sends nowhere near enough data to use up the bandwidth in the 5G recordings, so any controller comparison on those recordings is not yet meaningful.
hypotheses.source: Project-internal validity check for 5G-recording SCReAM / GCC experiments

established: The current ball-720p30 test video sends about 220–230 kbit / s, well below the typical bandwidth in the translated 5G recordings.
Earlier 5G-recording SCReAM / GCC comparisons cannot be read as meaningful algorithm comparisons.
Any future 5G-recording comparison must first pass this calibration with a test video that actually keeps the link busy.
limits: This shows the current test video is too light. It does not yet test a heavier replacement.
Brief low-capacity dips still happen in the handover-like recordings; the claim is about typical bandwidth across the whole replay.

hypotheses.title: SCReAM keeps more video watchable than GCC on tight 5G recordings
hypotheses.claim: On 5G recordings squeezed to one-third of their original capacity, SCReAM delivers more decoded frames to the viewer than GCC does, while the camera actually sends fewer bytes — on the two harder recordings (handover and resource-block).

established: On the high-capacity recording (CQI), both algorithms deliver nearly all frames; this recording acts as the easy control.
On the handover recording, SCReAM delivers about 2.7x as many frames to the viewer as GCC, while the camera sends fewer bytes.
On the resource-block recording, SCReAM delivers about 1.4x as many frames to the viewer as GCC, while the camera sends fewer bytes.
GCC's target bitrate does drop on the tighter recordings, but in this pipeline that lower target does not turn into fewer bytes leaving the camera.
The result is meaningful because the test video is now heavy enough to actually keep the recordings busy (the H3 calibration issue is fixed for this experiment).
limits: One test video, fixed recording, one set of bitrate bounds. The CQI recording shows SCReAM has no visible frame-delivery edge when the link has enough room for both algorithms.
The latency numbers still have a clock-skew artifact between aum and veda. H4's main claim is frame delivery and camera bytes, not latency.

hypotheses.title: Our SCReAM follows changing bandwidth; UMN's does not — because UMN's controller never reaches its encoder
hypotheses.claim: When the link's bandwidth keeps changing, our SCReAM raises and lowers its sending rate to match. UMN's reimplementation holds a nearly constant rate. The cause is a wiring problem inside UMN — the controller computes a target sending rate but that target is never applied to the video encoder — not a flaw in the SCReAM algorithm and not how often the loop runs.
hypotheses.source: Project-internal cross-implementation comparison vs UMN Teleop-Gopher-streamer (scream-integration branch 502533c)

environment.umn_stack: UMN Teleop-Gopher-streamer branch 502533c, congestion_controller=scream, network_time_sync on

established: On the high-capacity (CQI) recording, our SCReAM uses about 63% of the link; UMN uses about 22%.
UMN's SCReAM sends a nearly constant ~776–782 kbps across all three recordings, even though the recordings differ in capacity by about 2.5x. UMN is not tracking the link.
The cause is a wiring problem between the controller and the encoder, not the SCReAM algorithm and not how often the loop runs.

In code — UMN's encoder.py writes the controller's target rate onto an encoder that is already running. The libav library quietly ignores that write because a software encoder's bitrate is fixed when it opens. The libvpx path never reopens, so UMN's rate is effectively set once at startup.

Different shapes — UMN runs the controller in a separate thread that leaves a per-frame "budget" the encode loop has to apply by hand, per codec. Ours is a built-in pipeline element whose rate the framework applies to the encoder automatically.

Algorithm fidelity from reading the source (not measured here — the wiring problem hid it) — the reference SCReAM keeps track of how long the queue has been growing, how many bytes are in flight, and adapts its step size. UMN's just multiplies up by 1.05 or down by 0.8 on simple yes/no signals, with no memory.
An earlier version of this comparison showed UMN overshooting the link — that was a configuration mistake on our side (network_time_sync was off). With it on, UMN no longer overshoots.
UMN's delay-based congestion signal works once network_time_sync is on. Its loss-based signal never fired in these runs.
limits: Single-host loopback reproduces the bandwidth and the delay faithfully but not real 5G radio effects like interference or radio-layer retransmits.
We measured how much of the link each side uses, not how good the picture looks. "Uses the link better" is a bandwidth claim, not yet a video-quality claim.
UMN's controller is an early reimplementation (its own code marks receiver feedback as future work). This is a snapshot of branch 502533c, not a general statement about SCReAM.
We did not measure UMN's deployed hardware (NVENC) encoder. From reading the code we believe the same wiring problem affects it, but a real NVIDIA box would be the honest confirmation.
Measuring picture quality (PSNR or SSIM of the received video vs the source on both sides) is the next verification step.

hypotheses.title: SCReAM's queue-delay-target moves latency but not picture quality
hypotheses.claim: Turning SCReAM's queue-delay-target changes p95 latency on every network we tested, but does not change decoded picture quality (PSNR) — at this workload there is no quality gain to trade for the added latency.

established: The control loop responds the right way to the knob. As the knob goes from 10 ms to 500 ms on every network, p95 latency moves with it — tighter knob, less latency; looser knob, more latency. SCReAM is doing what its specification says it should.

The encoder does not benefit from extra room at this workload. Decoded picture quality (PSNR) stays roughly flat across the knob range — about a 1 dB swing on each network, which is within run-to-run noise at 3 reps. VP8 at the tested bitrates already has enough budget to encode this clip; loosening the knob does not give it useful extra room.
limits: Workload-specific. Tested with realmotion-avi (1280×1024 MJPEG, 10 fps, 60 s). A higher-motion or longer clip might saturate the encoder differently.
Bitrate-specific. Tested with init / min / max bitrate = 1500 / 200 / 4000 kbps. A tighter ceiling, or a more demanding source, might let the knob bite into quality.
The "no quality response" claim rests on PSNR. SSIM or VMAF might surface a smaller effect that PSNR misses.
3 reps per cell. PSNR effects smaller than about 1 dB are within noise.
Absolute latency numbers carry a clock-skew artifact between aum and veda (same one H4 flagged). The relative comparison across knob values within one sweep is unaffected.

hypotheses.title: With the encoder starved, the queue-delay-target knob starts trading picture quality
hypotheses.claim: H6 found the queue-delay-target knob moves latency but not picture quality, because the encoder had bytes to spare. With the bitrate ceiling dropped from 4000 to 800 kbps, the encoder is hungry, so loosening the knob should now raise picture quality (PSNR) as well as latency.

established: Starving the encoder did not turn the knob into a quality knob. With the ceiling dropped to 800 kbps, picture quality (PSNR) still stays flat as the knob loosens — about a 1 dB swing on each network, the same flat pattern H6 saw at 4000 kbps. So the queue-delay-target is a latency knob, not a quality knob, at both ceilings for this workload.
The robust takeaway across H6 and H7 is one finding, now tested twice -- the knob moves latency, not quality.
limits: Measurement caveat — read before trusting the absolute numbers: the PSNR values in H6 and H7 sit at 10–13 dB on every single cell. That is far below what a working pipeline should produce (a heavily compressed VP8 stream is normally 28–40 dB). A value near 10 dB is the signature of comparing misaligned frames — decoded frame N against source frame M not equal to N, or a resolution / colour-plane mismatch in the decoded_psnr truth pipeline.

What this caveat does and does not undermine. The relative finding (quality does not move with the knob) holds, because every cell uses the same metric and the comparison is internal. Any absolute quality claim is suspect until the metric is checked against a known-good baseline.

Next verification step is a one-cell sanity check — clean loopback, no impairment, near-lossless encode. If PSNR there is also ~10 dB the metric is misaligned and needs fixing; if it is ~40 dB the metric is sound and the stressed-network numbers are genuine.
Same workload and clock-skew caveats as H6.
